topic: Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement gives the law of conservation of mass?
items.correct: No atoms are lost or made, so the products have the same mass as the reactants.
items.misconception: Mass stays the same only when the reaction is run inside a sealed vessel.
items.why: Every classroom demonstration of constant mass uses a stopper or a sealed flask, so the seal gets remembered as a condition of the law rather than as a way of seeing it. Separate the law from the measurement. The seal changes what the balance can see, not what the atoms do; in an open vessel the atoms are all still there, just not all on the pan.
items.random_wrong: The number of molecules is unchanged, so the total mass cannot change.

items.q: 8.0 g of magnesium is burned in an open crucible and 13.3 g of magnesium oxide is left. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: 5.3 g of oxygen from the air has joined the magnesium in the crucible.
items.misconception: The heat energy taken in during the burning has added 5.3 g to the solid.
items.why: Heating is the only thing the student did, so it becomes the obvious cause, and energy is spoken about as something that goes into a substance and stays there. Write the equation: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The gain equals the mass of oxygen taken from the air, which can be predicted and then checked on the balance.
items.random_wrong: Extra magnesium atoms have been made, which is why the mass rose.

items.q: A student writes H2 + O2 -> H2O and is told it is not balanced. Which change balances it correctly?
items.correct: Write a 2 in front of H2 and a 2 in front of H2O, leaving O2 alone.
items.misconception: Change the product to H2O2 so that two oxygen atoms appear on the right.
items.why: Changing a subscript is the quickest way to make the counts agree, and students who see balancing as an arithmetic puzzle do not notice that they have changed the substance itself. Formulae are fixed by the substance and may never be altered. Only the multipliers written in normal script in front of a formula can be changed when balancing.
items.random_wrong: Write a 2 in front of O2 so that four oxygen atoms become available.

items.q: Why must a symbol equation be balanced?
items.correct: No atoms are lost or made, so each element has equal atoms per side.
items.misconception: So that the same number of molecules appears on both sides of the arrow.
items.why: The word balance suggests two equal piles, and the most visible things in an equation are the formulae rather than the atoms inside them. Make a table of elements and count atoms on each side. That is the only quantity balancing has to equalise.
items.random_wrong: So that the number of different substances shown matches on both sides.

items.q: In the formula 2Ca(NO3)2, what do the large 2 at the front and the small 2 after the bracket each do?
items.correct: The front 2 doubles the whole formula; the small 2 doubles the bracket only.
items.misconception: The front 2 shows two calcium atoms; the small 2 shows two nitrogen atoms.
items.why: The number sits immediately next to the first symbol, so proximity suggests it belongs to that symbol alone, exactly as a subscript does. Read the leading number as an instruction to write the formula out that many times. Doing so makes it obvious that every atom in the unit is multiplied.
items.random_wrong: The front 2 doubles only the calcium; the small 2 doubles the oxygen.

items.q: Calculate the relative formula mass of Ca(OH)2. Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1.
items.correct: 74, because the bracket doubles both the oxygen and the hydrogen.
items.misconception: 57, from adding 40, 16 and 1 with the bracket subscript ignored.
items.why: Students read a formula as a list of ingredients rather than as a count of atoms, and the subscripts are small and easy to skip when copying numbers down. Write out the atom count first, element by element, before adding anything, then multiply each relative atomic mass by that count.
items.random_wrong: 58, from doubling the hydrogen atoms but keeping one oxygen.

items.q: The relative atomic mass of oxygen is 16. What is the relative formula mass of O2?
items.correct: 32, because the molecule contains two atoms of oxygen.
items.misconception: 16, since that is the relative atomic mass given for oxygen.
items.why: The element is called oxygen and has one number in the data table, so the subscript in the molecular formula is read as part of the name rather than as a count of atoms. Ask how many atoms are in the particle. Elements that exist as molecules, such as O2, H2 and Cl2, have a relative formula mass of twice their relative atomic mass.
items.random_wrong: 8, because the two atoms in the molecule share the mass of 16.

items.q: For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO the reactants total (2 x 24) + 32 = 80. The Mr of MgO is 40. What is the product total?
items.correct: 80, since the same atoms are present on each side.
items.misconception: 40, because the relative formula mass of MgO is 40.
items.why: Relative formula mass is learned from single formulae, so students work out the Mr of MgO correctly and then stop, forgetting that the equation asks for the quantities shown. Multiply each Mr by the number in front of its formula before adding. The two totals then agree, which is the check that the equation is balanced.
items.random_wrong: 120, from adding the reactant total on to the product total.

items.q: Ammonium nitrate is NH4NO3, with Mr = 80. The relative atomic mass of nitrogen is 14. What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen?
items.correct: 35%, because the two nitrogen atoms give 28 out of the total of 80.
items.misconception: 22%, from the 2 nitrogen atoms among the 9 atoms in the formula.
items.why: Counting atoms is much easier than weighing them, and the word percentage suggests a share of a total number rather than a share of a total mass. Put the relative atomic masses in before dividing. Hydrogen atoms are numerous but light, so a count and a mass share give very different answers.
items.random_wrong: 17.5%, from using the mass of only one of the nitrogen atoms.

items.q: Which method gives the percentage by mass of an element in a compound?
items.correct: Multiply the Ar by the number of those atoms, divide by Mr, then x 100.
items.misconception: Divide the number of atoms of that element by the total atoms, then x 100.
items.why: Counting atoms is much easier than weighing them, and the word percentage suggests a share of a total number rather than a share of a total mass. Put the relative atomic masses in before dividing. Hydrogen atoms are numerous but light, so a count and a mass share give very different answers.
items.random_wrong: Divide the Mr of the compound by the Ar of that element, then x 100.

items.q: A weighed piece of copper is heated in an open crucible. The mass of the solid increases. Why?
items.correct: Oxygen from the air has combined with the copper to form copper oxide.
items.misconception: Heat energy absorbed from the flame has added to the mass of the metal.
items.why: Heating is the only thing the student did, so it becomes the obvious cause, and energy is spoken about as something that goes into a substance and stays there. Write the equation: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The gain equals the mass of oxygen taken from the air, which can be predicted and then checked on the balance.
items.random_wrong: The copper atoms expand as they get hot, so each one becomes much heavier.

items.q: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. The mass of the solid falls. Why?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide escapes, leaving copper oxide as the solid.
items.misconception: Some of the solid has been burned away by the heat of the Bunsen flame.
items.why: Everyday burning appears to consume things, and the residue really is lighter, so destruction looks like a reasonable description of what has happened. Collect the gas and weigh it. Its mass accounts exactly for the loss, showing that the atoms have moved rather than gone.
items.random_wrong: Mass is lost from the tube, so mass is not conserved in this reaction.

items.q: Use the particle model to explain why the balance reading falls when a metal carbonate is heated in an open tube.
items.correct: Carbon dioxide particles leave the tube and mix into the air, so they are no longer weighed.
items.misconception: The particles left in the tube move further apart, so the solid weighs less than before.
items.why: Density and mass are conflated, and the particle model is used to explain expansion far more often than it is used to explain mass. Separate spacing from number. Mass depends on how many particles are present and what they are, not on how far apart they sit.
items.random_wrong: Gas particles carry no mass of their own, so the reading falls as gas forms.

items.q: A student reads 25.00 cm3 from a burette, working carefully. Which statement about that measurement is correct?
items.correct: There is always some uncertainty about the result, however careful you are.
items.misconception: There is no uncertainty, because a burette is precise apparatus.
items.why: A digital or finely graduated display presents a definite-looking number, and the extra decimal places read as extra certainty. Ask two students to read the same burette and compare their answers. The spread makes the residual uncertainty visible.
items.random_wrong: Uncertainty appears only if the student misreads the burette scale.

items.q: Five titres are 24.8, 25.0, 25.1, 25.0 and 27.4 cm3. How should this set of results be handled?
items.correct: Plot all five, treat 27.4 as anomalous and leave it out of the mean.
items.misconception: Include all five in the mean, because a measured result may never be dropped.
items.why: Honesty about data is rightly stressed, and students hear excluding a point as cheating rather than as a judgement supported by the distribution itself. Report the anomaly and say why it was excluded. Identifying anomalies is part of representing the distribution, not a way of hiding it.
items.random_wrong: Average the highest and the lowest reading for the best estimate.

items.q: Four titres have a mean of 25.0 cm3, a lowest value of 24.8 cm3 and a highest of 25.2 cm3. How should the result be quoted?
items.correct: 25.0 plus or minus 0.2 cm3, which is half the range of 0.4 cm3.
items.misconception: 25.0 plus or minus 0.4 cm3, quoting the whole range as the uncertainty.
items.why: The range is the quantity that actually gets calculated, so it is the number to hand, and the halving step is easy to drop when the range is used about the mean. Draw the mean with the highest and the lowest values either side of it. The mean sits in the middle, so it is only half the range away from each end.
items.random_wrong: 24.8 plus or minus 0.2 cm3, using the lowest titre as the central value.

items.q: Marble chips and acid fizz in an open beaker and the balance reading falls by 0.8 g. Has mass been destroyed?
items.correct: No. The 0.8 g has left the beaker as carbon dioxide gas. Weigh the gas as well and the total is unchanged, because no atoms are lost or made.
items.misconception: When a gas bubbles away that mass has gone; the reaction has used it up, so mass really is lost.
items.why: Students trust the balance over the law. A gas is invisible and disperses, so it stops feeling like a substance at all, and the falling reading looks like direct evidence that matter has disappeared. Ask where the atoms went, not where the mass went. Every carbon and oxygen atom in the escaping gas came from the marble and the acid and still exists; the balance simply no longer has them on it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, is the number of molecules the same on both sides?
items.correct: No. Three molecules become two. It is the number of atoms of each element that is unchanged: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.
items.misconception: Mass is conserved because the number of molecules stays the same during a reaction.
items.why: Students read a formula as a single unbreakable object and count formulae rather than atoms, so conservation gets attached to the wrong quantity. Count atoms element by element on each side. Molecules are taken apart and rebuilt during a reaction, so their number often changes; the atoms are only rearranged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does conservation of mass apply to chemical reactions as well as to melting and dissolving?
items.correct: Yes. It applies to chemical reactions too, because atoms are rearranged rather than lost or made.
items.misconception: Mass is conserved in physical changes such as melting, but a chemical reaction makes a new substance so the mass can change.
items.why: A physical change obviously keeps the same stuff, while a reaction produces something visibly different, which makes it feel as though the amount of matter has changed too. Track the atoms through the change. New substances are new arrangements of the same atoms, so the total mass is fixed in both kinds of change.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an equation be balanced by adding a spare atom to whichever side is short?
items.correct: No. Every atom must belong to a formula, and formulae come in whole units set by the multiplier written in front of them.
items.misconception: If one side is one atom short you can simply add that atom on to make the counts agree.
items.why: Students treat the equation as a sum to be made to add up rather than as a description of real substances reacting. Ask what substance the extra atom would be. If it does not correspond to a real reactant or product it cannot be written; adjust the multipliers instead.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Ca(NO3)2 and in Ca(OH)2, what does the subscript 2 outside the bracket do?
items.correct: It multiplies everything inside the bracket: 2 nitrogen and 6 oxygen atoms in Ca(NO3)2, and 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms in Ca(OH)2.
items.misconception: The subscript after a bracket multiplies only the symbol written immediately before it, not the whole group.
items.why: Elsewhere a subscript does apply only to the symbol it follows, so students carry that rule across without noticing that this one follows a closing bracket. Treat the bracket as one package. A subscript after a closing bracket applies to the whole package, not to the last symbol inside it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Ca(OH)2, is the calcium doubled as well?
items.correct: No. The calcium sits outside the bracket, so the subscript does not reach it; only the O and the H inside are doubled.
items.misconception: The subscript after the bracket doubles every atom in the formula, so the calcium is doubled too.
items.why: It is the over-correction that follows once students have learned that a leading multiplier applies to everything, and the two kinds of number get merged. Compare the two positions directly. A number in normal script in front applies to the whole formula; a subscript applies only to what stands immediately before it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Nitrogen has Ar = 14 and NH4NO3 has Mr = 80. Is the percentage of nitrogen 14 / 80 x 100?
items.correct: No. There are two nitrogen atoms in the formula, so it is (2 x 14) / 80 x 100 = 35%.
items.misconception: Percentage by mass is the relative atomic mass of the element divided by the relative formula mass of the compound.
items.why: The remembered formula is Ar over Mr, and the step that multiplies by the number of atoms drops out because both numbers are handed to the student ready made. Count the atoms of that element in the formula first and write the multiplication down before dividing, even when the count turns out to be one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A reaction in an open flask loses mass. Does that break the law of conservation of mass?
items.correct: No. The law holds; the flask simply is not enclosing everything, so a gaseous product has left the balance without being weighed.
items.misconception: In a non-enclosed system mass genuinely is not conserved, so the law only applies to closed systems.
items.why: The balance reading is treated as the total mass of the reaction rather than as the mass of whatever happens to be sitting on the pan. Define the system before judging the law. Include the escaped gas in the accounting and the total is unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does carbon dioxide gas have mass?
items.correct: Yes. A cubic decimetre of carbon dioxide has a mass of about 1.8 g, and it is that mass the balance loses when the gas escapes.
items.misconception: Gases have no mass, or so little that they cannot account for a change on the balance.
items.why: Gases are invisible, they rise away, and nothing in everyday experience makes them feel heavy, so weightlessness becomes the default assumption. Weigh a sealed flask before and after filling it with carbon dioxide, or weigh a filled gas syringe, to make the mass of a gas concrete.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does repeating a measurement three times remove the uncertainty?
items.correct: No. Repeats let you estimate the uncertainty from the spread of the results, but some uncertainty always remains.
items.misconception: Once a measurement has been repeated and a mean taken, the result is certain.
items.why: Repeating is taught as the fix for unreliable data, so it is remembered as something that removes the problem rather than as something that measures it. Use the repeats to quote a range about the mean. The answer improves and gains an uncertainty; it does not lose one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a student takes a reading carefully and makes no mistakes, is the result free from uncertainty?
items.correct: No. Uncertainty is not the same as a mistake. It is present in every measurement, even one taken perfectly.
items.misconception: Uncertainty only appears when the experimenter has done something wrong.
items.why: In everyday speech uncertain suggests careless or unsure, so the word is heard as a criticism of the person rather than as a property of the measurement. Distinguish a mistake, which can be eliminated, from uncertainty, which is the unavoidable doubt about where the true value lies.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an equation balanced so that the energy given out equals the energy taken in?
items.correct: No. Balancing is a count of atoms of each element on each side. Energy is conserved too, but that is not what the numbers in an equation record.
items.misconception: A symbol equation is balanced in order to make the energy on each side of the arrow equal.
items.why: Conservation of mass and conservation of energy are taught close together and share the word conserved, so the reason for balancing gets attached to the wrong conserved quantity. Ask what the numbers in the equation actually count. They count atoms, and nothing in a symbol equation records energy at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The Ar of oxygen is 16. Is the Mr of O2 equal to 16 + 2?
items.correct: No. The subscript is a count of atoms, so it multiplies rather than adds: Mr = 2 x 16 = 32.
items.misconception: The subscript in a formula is added to the relative atomic mass when working out a relative formula mass.
items.why: Relative formula mass is introduced as a sum, so every number in sight gets added, and a small subscript looks like just another number to include in the total. Write the atom count in words first, for example two oxygen atoms, then write 2 x 16. The subscript never enters the sum as itself.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: H2 + O2 -> H2O has too few oxygen atoms on the right. Does putting a 2 in front of O2 fix it?
items.correct: No. That makes the surplus worse. Balance it as 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
items.misconception: When an equation does not balance, increase the multiplier on the side that seems to need more of that element.
items.why: Students act on the impression that one element is short without recounting both sides, and doubling the reactant containing it feels like the obvious repair. Recount both sides after every change. Balancing is iterative, and each new multiplier has to be checked against every element, not just the one being fixed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
